slides.title: Chapter 11: Organizing Files
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter moves from one file to whole folders: copy, move, delete, walk and archive. Every code slide shows the code, a plain explanation, and what the run printed as a table, chart or drawing. The same examples run on the chapter page.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts: copying and moving, safe deletion, folder trees, ZIP archives, and programs. Each code slide has its place in the chapter-code tab of the page, in this same order.

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions to carry through the chapter. Which operations change the disk for good, and how can a program show what it will do first? And how do we visit every file of a tree, and pack it into one archive?

slides.title: Part 1: Copying and moving
slides.say: Part one. Copy keeps the original, move does not. Copytree takes a whole folder. Watch what each function returns.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: copying and moving
slides.say: Copy is a photocopier, move is carrying the original. Copytree copies a whole binder. Ask which function returns the new path.

slides.title: shutil.copy: one file to a folder or a new name
slides.say: Copy keeps the original. A folder as target keeps the name; a file name as target renames the copy. The return value is the new path.

slides.title: shutil.copytree: a folder with everything in it
slides.say: Copytree needs a target that does not exist. A second call is refused. Dirs exist ok merges into the existing folder.

slides.title: copy and copy2: what happens to the time stamp
slides.say: Copy2 keeps the modification time, plain copy does not. We fix the time first so the run is repeatable.

slides.title: shutil.move: move, rename, overwrite
slides.say: Move relocates and renames in one call. Moving onto an existing file silently overwrites it. The source is gone afterwards.

slides.title: Part 2: Deleting, and staying safe
slides.say: Part two. Deleting cannot be undone. Learn the permanent functions, then the habit of printing before deleting.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: deleting safely
slides.say: Unlink is a shredder, send2trash is the basket beside it. A dry run reads the list aloud before shredding.

slides.title: os.unlink and os.rmdir: one file, one empty folder
slides.say: Unlink deletes one file for good, rmdir only an empty folder. There is no recycle bin. The first error is caught and explained.

slides.title: shutil.rmtree: a folder and everything inside
slides.say: Rmtree removes a whole tree at once. Use ignore errors when a missing folder is fine. Predict the three items before the run.

slides.title: Safe deletion: print first, delete later
slides.say: Print first, delete later. A typo in the pattern shows up as the wrong list, while nothing is lost. Comment the delete line back in only when the list is right.

slides.title: send2trash: the recycle bin
slides.say: Send2trash is a third-party module, not in the standard library, so it is not run on the page. It moves to the recycle bin instead of deleting for good.

slides.title: Story: the recycle bin is a 1983 drawing
slides.say: Susan Kare drew the trash can in 1983. The send2trash module moves a file to that bin. Ask: which of this chapter's functions can still be undone, and which cannot?

slides.title: Part 3: Folders and trees
slides.say: Part three. List one folder, then walk a whole tree. The walk gives three things at every step. We also build folders.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: folder trees
slides.say: A caretaker walks every floor. The walk gives each room, its inner rooms and its files. Mkdir builds a new room.

slides.title: Listing one folder: listdir, iterdir, glob
slides.say: Listdir gives names, iterdir gives Path objects, glob stays in one folder, rglob goes into all subfolders. Sorting makes the order repeatable.

slides.title: os.walk: the folder, its subfolders, its files
slides.say: Each step of os.walk gives the folder, its subfolders and its files. Sorting the subfolder list fixes the order. Bottom-up ends with the start folder.

slides.title: Counting bytes per folder while walking
slides.say: Walk the tree and add the file sizes per folder. The bar chart shows bytes per folder. Ask which folder is larger.

slides.title: Path.mkdir: making folders, also in a chain
slides.say: Mkdir makes one folder and needs the parent. Parents true builds the chain. Exist ok true accepts an existing folder.

slides.title: Story: the folder tree is a 1965 Multics design
slides.say: Daley and Neumann described a tree of folders in 1965. Unix kept it, and os.walk still visits it folder by folder. Ask students to draw the tree of their own laptop.

slides.title: Part 4: ZIP archives
slides.say: Part four. A ZIP file packs many files into one. Write it, read it, extract from it, and use the one-call helpers.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: ZIP archives
slides.say: A ZIP is a vacuum-packed suitcase. ZipFile opens it, extract unpacks one item or all of them.

slides.title: zipfile.ZipFile: write a file into an archive
slides.say: Mode w starts a new archive. Deflate with level nine compresses repeated text very well. Compare the two bars.

slides.title: ZIP modes: read, append, exclusive
slides.say: Mode a adds to an archive, mode x refuses to overwrite one. Writestr stores text without a file on disk.

slides.title: extractall and extract: unpacking an archive
slides.say: Extractall unpacks everything and rebuilds subfolders. Extract unpacks one member into a folder it creates.

slides.title: shutil.make_archive and unpack_archive
slides.say: Make archive packs a folder in one call, unpack archive reverses it. The names inside keep the folder name.

slides.title: Story: the ZIP format was given away on 14 February 1989
slides.say: Phil Katz and Gary Conway released the ZIP format into the public domain on 14 February 1989. That openness is why zipfile can read archives from any tool. Ask students why a free format helps a programmer.

slides.title: Story: the engine under ZIP_DEFLATED shipped on 1 May 1995
slides.say: Gailly and Adler released zlib 0.9 on 1 May 1995. Python's zipfile uses it for the deflate method. Ask students what would break if compression were owned by one company.

slides.title: Part 5: Programs that organize files
slides.say: Part five. Four programs that use everything so far. Predict the output, then run each on the page.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: programs that organize files
slides.say: Practice programs are driving lessons on an empty car park. Each one combines walking, copying and patterns.

slides.title: Project 5: back a folder up into a numbered ZIP
slides.say: Project five. Find the first free number, walk the folder, write every file. Run it twice to get spam one and spam two.

slides.title: Practice program: copy every PDF of a tree
slides.say: Walk a tree and copy only the PDFs. Lower makes the test ignore capitals. The source keeps all four files.

slides.title: Practice program: find the big files
slides.say: Walk everything and keep files above a size limit. The chart shows the sizes in bytes, biggest first.

slides.title: Practice program: American dates to European dates
slides.say: Swap month and day in file names with a pattern and shutil move. Files without a date stay as they are.

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: Python moves on. Path walk since 3.12, onexc in rmtree since 3.12, Path copy and move since 3.14. Run what the book printed, then check what changed.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart shows how many examples belong to each part.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills. Predict first, then run on the page. Ask students to explain each answer in one sentence.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter, then the Python documentation. The stories link to first-hand sources. Choose one link and read it before the next class.
